title: Ethics in Daily Life
summary: Values are the ideas and beliefs we hold as important; they are learnt from childhood from parents and surroundings and develop our conscience (the 'internal policeman'). Ethics test our values: the way we behave in difficult situations. Asif the taxi driver, who returned a briefcase full of cash and documents, shows honesty, truthfulness and responsibility. Every workplace and profession has its own ethics. Values of life: honesty and loyalty; respect for work; punctuality, regularity and discipline; courtesy and politeness; judicious use of resources; taking initiative; efficiency. Values at the workplace: honesty and loyalty to the organisation; respect for the assigned work; punctuality, regularity and discipline; judicious use of resources; courtesy to co-workers; efficiency; willingness to take up new tasks.
## Need for ethics, rights and responsibilities

If values are not practised: loss of life and damage to public property, breakdown of families, no law and order, crime and corruption, alcohol and drug abuse, abuse of women, children and vulnerable people, wastage of resources, and total imbalance in society. We all live in a family where we learn caring, sharing, tolerance and empathy. Rights and responsibilities go together; only then are there peace and harmony (Ankita's story: if you are rude and uncooperative others will treat you in the same way).
## Caring and respecting others; good manners

Respect must be given to be received; it is alright to disagree, but express it politely – expressing views is your right, doing it respectfully is your duty. Signs of disrespect: not greeting everyone in a room, not taking leave of elders, not introducing friends to the family, raising the voice with elders, going out without informing or changing the TV channel without caring for others, staying away on important family days. Good manners: speak cheerfully; think before you speak; do not interrupt when two people are talking; never speak ill of others; be respectful when talking to parents; converse in a language understood by all in the group (it is rude to use one nobody understands); be humble when talking about yourself; do not whisper while sitting in a group.

All forms of work, manual or intellectual, are labour; dignity of labour means all jobs are respected equally and no occupation is superior to another; respectability lies in how well the work is done, not in its kind. A sweeper who does his work well is more honourable than an official who neglects duty or earns unfairly. Examples: the Prophet asking a beggar to buy an axe and sell wood; Guru Nanak preferring dry bread earned by the carpenter Bhai Lalo's honest labour to the rich Malik Bhago's meal. It is better to earn one's own living by honest means.
## Tolerance, empathy, positive attitude and life skills

Life skills are 'the abilities for adaptive and positive behaviour that enable individuals to deal effectively with the demands and challenges of everyday life' (adaptive – flexible and able to adjust; positive – forward-looking). Empathy is the capacity to recognise and share the feelings experienced by others (the boy who chose the limping puppy). Tolerance is the ability to accept opinions and practices different from your own, but it does not mean accepting injustice and corruption – tolerance of the wrong is a great evil. A positive attitude brings optimism, avoids negative thinking and worries, helps to cope with daily life and keeps relationships healthy (Mrs Gill). These are essential also in understanding people with special needs and senior citizens.

vsa: What can be the four consequences of not following values in the society?

Loss of life and damage to public property; crime and corruption; breakdown of families and loss of law and order; alcohol and drug abuse; abuse of women, children and vulnerable people; wastage of resources.
List any four essential values that help to maintain a conducive atmosphere at home.
Honesty and loyalty; respect for work; punctuality, regularity and discipline; courtesy and politeness; judicious use of resources; taking initiative; efficiency in completing tasks.
Mention any four expected ethics in a nurse.
Honesty and truthfulness; punctuality and regularity; empathy and care for patients; courtesy and politeness; respect for work and confidentiality; efficiency in completing tasks.
Define values and ethics with one example.

Values are the ideas and beliefs we hold as important and learn from parents and surroundings, e.g. caring for others. Ethics are the way we behave in difficult situations that test our values, e.g. the taxi driver returning the briefcase he found.
Why is dignity of labour important?
All jobs are respected equally; respectability lies in how well work is done, not its kind; it encourages people to earn their living honestly instead of depending on others or begging.
How can we show respect to our elders? (any four)
Greet them; take leave of them; introduce friends to them; speak politely and avoid a raised voice; inform them before going out; consider their wishes while using the TV; disagree politely.
Write two good manners in conversation.
Do not interrupt when two people are talking; converse in a language understood by all; speak cheerfully and think before speaking.
sa: What is the importance of ethics in our daily life? Explain.

Values and ethics are the base of our actions and behaviour. If they are practised there is peace, law and order and respect for rights and responsibilities. Without them there will be crime, corruption, breakdown of families, drug abuse, abuse of the vulnerable and wastage of resources, so it is each person's responsibility to live ethically; at the workplace ethics (honesty, punctuality, loyalty, courtesy) create a conducive atmosphere.
Explain tolerance, empathy and positive attitude with one example each.

Tolerance is the ability to accept opinions and practices different from our own (but not injustice or corruption). Empathy is the capacity to recognise and share the feelings of others – the little boy chose the limping puppy so that it would not be lonely. A positive attitude brings optimism and helps to cope with daily life – Mrs Gill pointed out one good quality in each of her naughty students and they became achievers.
Describe the values of life that help to maintain a good atmosphere in the family (any six).
Honesty and loyalty; respect for work; punctuality, regularity and discipline; courtesy and politeness; judicious use of resources; taking initiative; efficiency in completing tasks.
la: Explain the signs of showing respect and disrespect to elders and five good manners.

Disrespect: not greeting everyone in a room; not taking leave of elders; not introducing friends to the family; raising the voice in arguments; going out without informing or changing the TV channel without caring for others; staying away on important family days. Respect: greeting everyone, taking leave, introducing friends, speaking politely, informing elders. Good manners: speak cheerfully; think before you speak; do not interrupt; never speak ill of others; speak in a language understood by all; be humble; do not whisper in a group.
Explain dignity of labour with examples and why we should not depend on others.

Dignity of labour means that all work, manual or intellectual, is respected equally and no occupation is considered superior; respectability lies in doing the work well. Krishna the cobbler worked at 70 to earn his meal in a dignified manner; the Prophet asked a beggar to cut and sell wood; Guru Nanak preferred the dry bread earned by honest labour. It is better to earn one's living honestly than to depend on others.
